title: Game development with Unity for beginners
summary: A first course in making games for students who have never coded. They build three small games by following along, then design, build, playtest and share one of their own.
brief:
Game development with Unity for complete beginners: a 14-week asynchronous online course for undergraduates, 3 credits, about 9 hours of work a week. Students have never written code and never made a game. They work alone on their own Windows or Mac computer; there are no live sessions, and a student who follows the week's page with nobody to ask must be able to finish the week. Software, all free: Unity 6.6 (editor 6000.6) installed through Unity Hub with a Unity Personal license, and Visual Studio Code with the Unity extension for writing C#. Projects start from the Universal 3D template, except the 2D game, which starts from the Universal 2D template. Version facts every page must respect: new projects use the Input System package only, so the old Input class (Input.GetAxis, Input.GetKey) throws an error and input is read with Keyboard.current or an InputAction; a Rigidbody's velocity is linearVelocity; on-screen text is TextMeshPro; an object is found with FindAnyObjectByType. My attached version notes list the exact menu names and code for this version: follow them. Students build three small games by following along, then one of their own. Game 1, Orb Collector (weeks 2 to 5): roll a ball around an arena, collect spinning pickups, show a score and a win message. Game 2, Dodge (weeks 6 to 9): move a player to avoid hazards that spawn faster and faster, with lives, game over and restart, sound, particles, and a start menu. Game 3, Hop (weeks 10 and 11): a 2D platformer with a tilemap level, jumping, sprite animation and collectibles. Weeks 12 to 14: each student designs, builds, playtests and shares a small game of their own. Week by week: 1, setting up Unity and a tour of the Editor, building a small scene from primitive shapes; 2, GameObjects and components, materials and light, physics with Rigidbody and colliders; 3, the first C# script: variables, Start and Update, the Console and how to read an error; 4, input and movement: vectors, forces, FixedUpdate, a camera that follows; 5, collisions, triggers and scoring: if statements, tags, counting, text on screen, winning; 6, prefabs and spawning: Instantiate, random positions, timers, destroying objects; 7, game state and UI: lives, game over, restart, methods, buttons; 8, sound, particles and game feel; 9, menus and scenes, building the game so a classmate can run it on Windows or Mac, then finishing and playtesting Dodge with a twist of your own; 10, 2D: sprites, tilemaps, 2D physics, running and jumping; 11, 2D animation, collectibles and a camera that follows, and the proposal for your own game; 12, scoping and prototyping your own game, and how to debug; 13, playtesting with classmates, iterating and polishing; 14, showcase, reflection, and what to learn next. Every week has the same shape: a guided build that leaves something working on screen, a challenge without steps, a self-check quiz, a forum post that shares a screenshot or short clip of the build (and replies after trying two classmates' ideas), and something to submit. Grading: weekly builds 40% (submitted as a short screen recording and a screenshot), forum participation 15%, the Dodge game with your own twist, due in week 9, 15%, and the final game project 30% (proposal in week 11, playable prototype in week 12, final build and showcase post in week 14), with rubrics for the two games.
Before planning, the teacher answered:
- Should Orb Collector and Dodge be built with 3D keyboard controls, or should Dodge move the player on a flat plane? Both 3D; Dodge uses a flat arena with top-down keyboard movement
- Where will students get the art and sound for Dodge and Hop in weeks 8 to 11? Folio points to free CC0 packs, such as Kenney
- How are the weekly build, forum post and challenge submitted and graded in the course platform? Upload to the LMS; graded complete or incomplete

blocks.text: Welcome. In this course you will make games in Unity, even if you have never written code or built a game. You start with a small scene made of simple shapes. Over the term you build three small games by following along, then design, build, test and share a game of your own. You work alone, at your own pace, on your own computer, and there are no live sessions. Each week has its own page that tells you everything you need, so if you follow it you can finish the week without asking anyone. If you get stuck, the forum is there, and the instructor reads it.

Put the week in the title of your post. If you solve it yourself, post how, because it helps the next student.

l_c1af38aae15b.title: Set up Unity and build a scene
l_c1af38aae15b.summary: Install Unity and Visual Studio Code, tour the Editor, and build a scene from primitive shapes; submit a screen recording and screenshot.
keyIdeas: The Editor is a set of windows, and each answers one question: what is in my scene (Hierarchy), what does it look like (Scene and Game views), what are its settings (Inspector), what files do I have (Project window) and what went wrong (Console).
Everything in a scene is a GameObject, and its Transform says where it is, how it is turned and how big it is. Typing exact Transform numbers lets you rebuild the same scene on any computer.
What the Game view shows depends on three things together: the camera’s position and rotation, its field of view, and the shape of the Game view itself.
Capturing your screen, as a picture and as a short recording, is a skill you will use all term, so you learn it on a small scene.

study.overview: You can now get Unity 6.6 and Visual Studio Code running, open a Universal 3D project, name the five windows you will use every week, and build a scene by typing exact Transform numbers. You also know how to frame the Main Camera and capture your work as a screenshot and a short recording. Reread this page before next week, when you give these shapes components, materials and light.

points.heading: Name the Editor window that answers your question
points.explanation: The Editor is a set of windows, and each answers one question. The Hierarchy lists what is in your scene. The Scene and Game views show what it looks like: Scene is where you build, and Game is what the player sees through the Main Camera. The Inspector shows the settings of whatever you have selected. The Project window holds your files, and the Console shows what went wrong. Example: you want the settings of Tower. Click Tower in the Hierarchy, then read its Transform in the Inspector. If a window goes missing, choose Window > Layouts > Default.

points.heading: Place any GameObject with its Transform
points.explanation: Everything in a scene is a GameObject, and its Transform holds Position (where its centre is), Rotation (how far it is turned, in degrees) and Scale (how big it is, as a multiplier). Position is the centre, so a shape rests on the ground when its Position Y is half its height after scaling. Example: a Cylinder is 2 units tall at Scale 1, so at Scale Y 3 it is 6 units tall and Tower needs Position Y 3. A Cube at Scale Y 3 is 3 tall, so its centre is at 1.5, as with Wall_Back. Typing the same numbers rebuilds the same scene on any computer. New objects appear where the Scene view is looking, so type their Position values first.

points.heading: Control what the Game view shows
points.explanation: The Game view depends on three things together: the camera’s position and rotation, its Field of View, and the shape of the Game view. Change any one and the picture changes. Example: with Game view set to 16:9 Aspect, Field of View 60, and the Main Camera at Position 0, 16, -16 with Rotation 45, 0, 0, the whole 20 by 20 courtyard fits in the picture. If the picture is cropped, check the aspect first, then each camera number in turn. Before you press Play, remember that Play runs the scene like a player, so click it again to stop before you edit. Changes made during Play are thrown away.

points.heading: Capture your work as a picture and a recording
points.explanation: You will show your work this way all term, so it is worth doing well now. Put Unity in the state you want to show: the Courtyard scene open, the Game tab selected, 16:9 Aspect and Play not pressed. Take a screenshot of the whole Editor. Then record about ten seconds of pressing Play, watching and pressing Play again. Open both files to check them. The picture should show the framed courtyard, and the recording should play. Both are what you submit for this week’s Weekly builds.

page.text: Every game you make this term lives inside the Unity Editor, so this week you get it running and learn your way around. This is where the course starts, so there is nothing to catch up on. Then you will build a small walled courtyard from simple shapes, placing each one by typing exact numbers. By Sunday night you will have a saved scene called Courtyard that shows everything in one view, and you will know how to capture it as a screenshot and a screen recording.

page.transcript:
Hello, and welcome. Over this term you will make games in Unity, a free tool that real studios use for everything from phone games to big releases. You do not need to have written code or made a game before. If you can follow a page carefully, you can do this.

Here is how the course works. Every week is a page like this one. You work through it alone, whenever suits you. I do not lecture. I post an announcement at the start of the week, I answer questions in the forum, and I give feedback on your work. The page is written so you can finish the week without asking anyone. Each part ends with a checkpoint that tells you what you should see on screen, and what it looks like when something has gone wrong.

The rhythm is the same all term. Your first forum post is due on Thursday. Replies and everything else are due on Sunday night. Start early. Installing Unity means a big download, and that is the slowest part of this week.

What will you make? You will build small games by following along. First, a game where you roll a ball around an arena and collect spinning pickups. Then a game where you dodge hazards that fall faster and faster. Then a platformer in two dimensions. After that you design, build, test and share a small game of your own.

This week is about the ground you stand on. You will install Unity Hub, the launcher that manages your Unity versions, and then Unity 6.6 itself. You will install Visual Studio Code, where you will write code later in the course. Then you will create a project and learn the windows. The Hierarchy lists everything in your scene. The Scene view is where you look around and build. The Game view shows what a player will see. The Inspector shows the settings of whatever you have selected. The Project window holds your files, and the Console, beside it, shows messages.

Then you will build a small walled courtyard from simple shapes. Every object has a Transform, which is its position, its rotation and its scale. You will type exact numbers instead of dragging. Numbers are the same on your screen and mine, so when the page says the tower sits at 0, 3, 0, yours will too.

One habit before you start: save often. In Unity that is Control S on Windows, or Command S on a Mac. Now go on to the next part.

page.text: How the course is graded

items: Weekly builds: 40% of the course grade.
Forum participation: 15%.
Dodge game with your own twist: 15%.
Final game project: 30%.

page.text: How each week runs

Each week is one page like this. Your first forum post is due by Thursday. Replies and all other work are due by Sunday night. The instructor posts an announcement at the start of the week, answers questions in the forum and gives feedback on your work. Next week’s page opens on the same pattern.
What you need

items: A Windows or Mac computer of your own, with a keyboard and mouse. A trackpad works, but a mouse with a scroll wheel makes the Scene view easier.
A reliable internet connection for large downloads this week.
About 20 GB of free disk space for Unity, your projects and your recordings.
An email address you can check, for a free Unity ID.
No coding and no game experience. All the software is free: Unity Hub, Unity 6.6 with a Unity Personal license, and Visual Studio Code.

page.text: This page is written for Unity 6.6 (editor 6000.6, shown as 6000.6.4f1 in the Editor’s title bar) and the Universal 3D template. A different 6000.6 patch number is fine. If your Editor is another version, such as 6.5 or 6.7, or your project uses another template, menus and fields will not match the page. Install 6.6 beside it from Unity Hub and use that one for the whole course. If Unity Hub ever offers to upgrade a project to another version, say no.
Make your course folder
A folder keeps every project in one place you can find. The steps differ by system, so follow the one for yours.
On Windows

items.text: Press the Windows key and E together to open **File Explorer**.
In the list on the left, click **Documents**.
Right-click an empty space in the main area and choose **New** > **Folder**.
Type UnityCourse and press Enter.

page.text: You should see a folder named UnityCourse inside Documents. It is empty for now. If it is missing, you probably created it inside another folder, so open that folder and look there.

Install Unity Hub, add your license and install Unity 6.6

On a Mac, double-click the downloaded .dmg file and drag **Unity Hub** onto the **Applications** folder.
Open Unity Hub.
Click **Sign in**, then create a free Unity ID or sign in with the one you have, and follow the prompts.
Click the gear at the top right to open **Settings**.
Click **Licenses**.
Click **Add license**.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
1. The progress bar stops moving, or the install shows as failed. Fix: check your connection and free disk space, then use the retry option on the entry, or choose **Install Editor** again. The install resumes.

2. Hub says there is no license, or a project later refuses to open. Fix: in **Settings** > **Licenses** choose **Add license** again, and make sure you are signed in with the same Unity ID as before.

3. Your computer is managed by a school or employer and will not let you install. Fix: ask the IT help desk to install Unity Hub and Unity 6.6, and say so in the forum so others can help.
Install Visual Studio Code and its Unity extension
You will write C# code in Visual Studio Code from later in the course, and installing it now means the tool is ready when you need it.

items.text: In your web browser, go to **code.visualstudio.com**.
Click the download button for your system.
On Windows, run the downloaded installer and accept the defaults, clicking **Next**, then **Install**, then **Finish**.
On a Mac, open the downloaded zip file and drag **Visual Studio Code** onto the **Applications** folder.
Open Visual Studio Code. On a Mac, click **Open** if it asks whether you are sure.
In the bar down the left edge, click the **Extensions** icon, or press Control, Shift and X (Windows) or Shift, Command and X (Mac).
Click the search box at the top and type Unity.
In the results, find the extension named **Unity** whose publisher is Microsoft, and click **Install**.
Wait until the button changes from **Install** to a button that says **Uninstall**. If a prompt asks you to sign in, you can dismiss it for now.

page.text: The Unity extension should appear in your installed extensions, and its page should show **Uninstall** rather than **Install**. Visual Studio Code may also have added a C# extension by itself, which is normal. If you still see **Install**, the install did not finish: click it again and wait.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
1. On a Mac, a message says the app cannot be opened because Apple cannot check it for malicious software. Fix: in **Applications**, right-click **Visual Studio Code**, choose **Open**, then click **Open** again.

2. The search shows many results named Unity. Fix: choose the one published by Microsoft. Extensions with similar names, such as snippet packs, are different.

3. On Windows, the installer asks for permission and fails on a managed computer. Fix: ask your IT help desk, or download the User Installer from the same page.
Create the Courtyard project and tour the Editor
A project holds everything about one game, and the Editor’s windows are where you will work all term, so you create a project now and learn the name of every window.
Create the project

Click **New project**.
At the top of the screen, check that the Editor version reads 6000.6.4f1, or another 6000.6 version.

page.text: Build the courtyard from primitive shapes
Every game scene is made of GameObjects, and the quickest way to learn them is to place a few by exact numbers, so you will build the courtyard one shape at a time.

A GameObject is anything that exists in a scene, such as a camera, a light or a cube. A primitive is a ready-made basic shape: cube, sphere, capsule, cylinder or plane. Every GameObject has a Transform, which holds three things. Position says where the object’s centre is, in units along X (right), Y (up) and Z (forward). Rotation says how far it is turned, in degrees. Scale says how big it is, as a multiplier of its normal size.

Here is why numbers beat dragging. A Cylinder is 2 units tall at Scale 1. At Scale Y of 3 it is 6 units tall. Position is the centre, so for it to stand on the ground at Y 0, its centre must be half of 6, which is 3. Type 3 and it stands exactly on the ground, on your screen and on every other student’s.
Name the scene, then place the ground and the tower

items.text: Choose **File** > **Save As...**.

Type Courtyard as the name. Save it inside the Scenes folder: if the box shows Assets, open **Scenes** first (on a Mac, click the arrow beside **Where** to see the folders). Then click **Save**. The title bar now starts with Courtyard.
Choose **GameObject** > **3D Object** > **Plane**.
Type Ground and press Enter. The name is already in edit mode. A yellow note about the Plane’s Mesh Collider may show in the Inspector: it is harmless, so leave it.
In the **Inspector**, in the **Transform** section, set **Position** to 0, 0, 0. Click the **X** box, type 0, press Tab to jump to **Y**, type 0, press Tab, type 0.
Set **Rotation** to 0, 0, 0.
Set **Scale** to 2, 1, 2. The plane is now 20 by 20 units.

shot.alt: The Transform of Ground with Position 0, 0, 0, Rotation 0, 0, 0 and Scale 2, 1, 2.
shot.shows: The Inspector only, with Ground selected, showing the Transform with Position 0, 0, 0, Rotation 0, 0, 0 and Scale 2, 1, 2. Outline the three rows of values.

items.text: Choose **GameObject** > **3D Object** > **Cylinder**.
Type Tower and press Enter.
In the **Inspector**, set **Position** to 0, 3, 0.
Set **Rotation** to 0, 0, 0.
Set **Scale** to 2, 3, 2.

shot.alt: The Transform of Tower with Position 0, 3, 0, Rotation 0, 0, 0 and Scale 2, 3, 2.
shot.shows: The Inspector only, with Tower selected, showing the Transform with Position 0, 3, 0, Rotation 0, 0, 0 and Scale 2, 3, 2. Outline the three rows of values.

page.shows: The whole Editor after Tower is placed. The Scene view shows the flat Ground with the Tower standing in its middle, and the Hierarchy lists Ground and Tower under Courtyard. Outline the Hierarchy entries.

page.text: The Scene view should show a flat square with a tall cylinder standing in its middle. The Hierarchy should list Ground and Tower. If the tower floats or is half sunk into the ground, select Tower and check that **Position** Y is 3. If the ground looks tiny, check that **Scale** is 2, 1, 2.
Add the walls, crates, ball and guard
Six more objects, each made the same way. Here are their values.

items: Wall_Back: Cube, Position 0, 1.5, 10, Rotation 0, 0, 0, Scale 20, 3, 1
Wall_Left: Cube, Position -10, 1.5, 0, Rotation 0, 0, 0, Scale 1, 3, 20
Crate_A: Cube, Position 5, 0.5, -3, Rotation 0, 0, 0, Scale 1, 1, 1
Crate_B: Cube, Position 6.5, 0.75, -4.5, Rotation 0, 30, 0, Scale 1.5, 1.5, 1.5
Ball: Sphere, Position -5, 0.5, -4, Rotation 0, 0, 0, Scale 1, 1, 1
Guard: Capsule, Position -6, 1, -1, Rotation 0, 0, 0, Scale 1, 1, 1

items.text: Choose **GameObject** > **3D Object**, then the shape named in the list.
Type the object’s name and press Enter.
In the **Inspector**, set **Position** to the values in the list.
Set **Rotation** to the values in the list.
Set **Scale** to the values in the list.

page.title: Why those Y values
page.text: Each object’s Y position is half its height after scaling. A cube is 1 unit tall, so at Scale Y 3 it is 3 tall and its centre is at 1.5. A sphere or capsule works the same way: the Ball is 1 unit tall and sits at 0.5, and the Guard is 2 units tall and sits at 1. That keeps every object resting on the ground instead of floating or sinking.

items.text: Press Control and S (Windows) or Command and S (Mac) to save the scene.

page.alt: A Hierarchy with eleven entries and a Scene view showing a square ground, a central tower, two walls, two crates, a ball and a capsule.
page.shows: The whole Editor. The Hierarchy lists Main Camera, Directional Light, Global Volume, Ground, Tower, Wall_Back, Wall_Left, Crate_A, Crate_B, Ball and Guard. The Scene view is pulled back far enough to show every object. Outline the Hierarchy list.

page.text: The Hierarchy should list Ground, Tower, Wall_Back, Wall_Left, Crate_A, Crate_B, Ball and Guard under the camera, light and volume. In the Scene view, the two walls should meet at one corner of the ground, the crates should stand on the right and the ball and capsule on the left. If an object is missing, check the Hierarchy for it. If one floats or sinks, select it and compare its Position Y with the list. A title ending in an asterisk means the scene is not saved yet.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
1. A new object appears at an odd position. Fix: that is normal, because new objects appear where the Scene view is looking. Type the Position values from the list.

2. You typed a value into the wrong box, so a wall is lying flat or stretched. Fix: select it and compare the **Rotation** and **Scale** rows with the list.

3. You cannot find an object in the Scene view. Fix: click it in the Hierarchy, move the pointer over the Scene view and press F.
Frame the camera, press Play and save
The Game view is what a player sees, so you point the Main Camera at the courtyard and check that nothing is cut off.

The goal is one view that shows the whole Ground, both walls and every object, in a Game view set to the 16:9 shape. Three things decide that together: where the camera is and which way it points, its field of view (how wide it sees, in degrees), and the shape of the Game view. Change any one and the picture changes. With a field of view of 60, a camera at 0, 16, -16 and tilted down 45 degrees fits the whole 20 by 20 courtyard, with the near edge of the ground a little above the bottom of the picture.

items.text: Click the **Game** tab.
In the bar along the top of the **Game** view, open the third dropdown, which reads **Free Aspect**, and choose **16:9 Aspect**.

shot.alt: The Game view toolbar with the aspect dropdown open and 16:9 Aspect selected.
shot.shows: The top of the Game view with the aspect dropdown open and 16:9 Aspect chosen. Outline the dropdown. Capture on Windows or Mac, and say which.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy** window, click **Main Camera**.
In the **Inspector**, in the **Transform** section, set **Position** to 0, 16, -16.
Set **Rotation** to 45, 0, 0.
Set **Scale** to 1, 1, 1.
In the **Inspector**, scroll down to the **Camera** section and find **Field of View**.
Set **Field of View** to 60.

shot.alt: The Main Camera Inspector with Position 0, 16, -16, Rotation 45, 0, 0, Scale 1, 1, 1 and Field of View 60.
shot.shows: The Inspector only, with Main Camera selected: Transform with Position 0, 16, -16, Rotation 45, 0, 0, Scale 1, 1, 1, and the Camera section scrolled into view with Field of View 60. Outline all of those values.

items.text: Look at the **Game** view.

page.title: Why three settings
page.text: Field of view is how wide an angle the camera sees. A larger number sees more of the scene but makes everything smaller, and a smaller number zooms in. The Game view’s own shape matters too: a narrower view has less room on each side, which is why you chose 16:9 first.

page.alt: The Game view of the Courtyard in 16:9 with the whole ground, the tower, both walls, both crates, the ball and the capsule inside the picture and nothing cut off.
page.shows: The Game view only, aspect 16:9 Aspect, Play not pressed. The whole Ground is inside the picture: its near edge a little above the bottom of the view, its far edge behind Wall_Back, and its left and right edges inside the sides. Tower, Wall_Back, Wall_Left, Crate_A, Crate_B, Ball and Guard are all fully visible.

page.text: In the Game view you should see the whole ground with all four of its edges inside the picture, the tower in the middle, both walls, both crates, the ball and the capsule, with plain background around it. If anything is cut off, check these in order: the Game view says 16:9 Aspect; Position is exactly 0, 16, -16; Rotation is exactly 45, 0, 0; Field of View is exactly 60.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
1. The picture is cropped at the sides or bottom. Fix: the Game view is probably not set to 16:9 Aspect, so choose it again from the dropdown.

2. The view is far too zoomed in or out. Fix: Field of View is not 60. If the **Camera** section shows a focal length instead, a physical camera setting is on; untick **Physical Camera** and set **Field of View** to 60.

3. The Game view is a grey or blue empty picture. Fix: the camera points the wrong way. Check **Rotation** is 45, 0, 0 and that Position has a minus sign on the Z value.
Press Play and save

items.text: At the top centre of the Editor, click the **Play** button.
Watch the **Game** view for ten seconds. It stays still, because nothing in the scene moves yet.
Click the **Play** button again to stop.
Press Control and S (Windows) or Command and S (Mac) to save the scene.

page.alt: Play is clicked, the Game view shows the still courtyard for ten seconds, and Play is clicked again to stop.
page.caption: Play is clicked, the button turns into a square while the game runs, and a second click stops it.
page.shows: The whole Editor, silent, with the Game tab selected at 16:9 Aspect. The pointer clicks Play at the top centre, the Editor tints, ten seconds pass with the courtyard unchanged, then the pointer clicks Play again and the tint goes. Under thirty seconds.

page.title: Why stop before editing
page.text: Play runs your scene the way a player would see it. Changes you make while Play is on are thrown away when you stop, so always click Play again to stop before you edit anything.
After saving, the title bar should show Courtyard with no asterisk, and the Play button should not be pressed. If the Play button shows a square, you are still in Play mode: click it once more.

If your Courtyard does not match, or you want to check your work, download the finished project for this week. Close the Unity Editor. In File Explorer or Finder, open UnityCourse and create a folder named CourtyardReference. In Unity Hub, add and open the extracted Courtyard folder inside CourtyardReference. Your own Courtyard project remains in its original folder. In the **Project** window, open **Assets** > **Scenes** and double-click **Courtyard** to open the finished scene. Then click the **Game** tab and set the aspect to **16:9 Aspect**, because that setting belongs to your Editor and is not stored in the project.

page.text: Take a screenshot and record your screen
Showing a game working means capturing a picture and a short recording of your screen, and you will do both all term, so you practise on the Courtyard now.

Before you start, put Unity in the state you want to capture: the Courtyard scene open, the Game tab selected, the aspect set to 16:9 Aspect and Play not pressed. Follow the steps for your system. The recording is a few seconds of you pressing Play, watching, and pressing Play again.
Screenshot on Windows

items.text: Click the Unity Editor window so it is in front, with the Game tab showing the framed courtyard.
Press the Windows key and PrintScreen together. On some laptops you also hold Fn. The screen dims for a moment.
Open **File Explorer** and click **Pictures** in the list on the left.
Open the **Screenshots** folder.
Double-click the newest file, named Screenshot with a number, and check that it shows the whole Editor.

page.text: Screenshot on a Mac

items.text: Click the Unity Editor window so it is in front, with the Game tab showing the framed courtyard.
Press Shift, Command and 3 together. A small preview appears in a corner of the screen.
On the Desktop, find the newest file named Screenshot followed by the date and time.
Double-click it and check that it shows the whole Editor.

page.text: Recording on Windows with Xbox Game Bar

items.text: Press the Windows key and I to open **Settings**, then click **Gaming**.
Open **Xbox Game Bar**, which is called **Game Bar** on Windows 11, and switch it on.
Click the Unity Editor window so it is the active window.
Press the Windows key and G together to open the Game Bar. If it asks whether this is a game, tick the box that says yes.
In the **Capture** widget, click the record button, the circle.
In Unity, click **Play**, wait ten seconds, then click **Play** again to stop.
Press the Windows key, Alt and R together to stop recording. A notification says the clip was recorded.
Open **File Explorer**, click **Videos**, open the **Captures** folder and double-click the newest .mp4 file to check it.

page.text: Recording on Windows 11 with Snipping Tool, if Game Bar will not record

items.text: Press the Windows key, type Snipping Tool and press Enter.
In the Snipping Tool toolbar, click the video camera icon to switch from pictures to recording.
Click **New**. The screen dims.
Drag a rectangle around the whole Unity Editor window.
Click **Start**. A short countdown runs, then recording begins.
In Unity, click **Play**, wait ten seconds, then click **Play** again to stop.
Click the stop button in the small recording bar.
In the preview that opens, click the **Save** icon, choose the **Videos** folder, type Courtyard-recording as the name and click **Save**.
Open **File Explorer**, click **Videos**, and double-click Courtyard-recording to check it plays.

page.text: Recording on a Mac

items.text: Press Shift, Command and 5 together. A toolbar appears at the bottom of the screen.
Click **Record Selected Portion**.
Drag the box that appears so it covers the whole Unity Editor window.
Click **Record**.
In Unity, click **Play**, wait ten seconds, then click **Play** again to stop.
Click the stop button in the menu bar at the top of the screen.
On the Desktop, double-click the newest file named Screen Recording followed by the date and time, and check that it plays.

page.alt: A screenshot of the full Unity Editor with Courtyard in the title bar, the Hierarchy listing Ground, Tower, Wall_Back, Wall_Left, Crate_A, Crate_B, Ball and Guard, and the Game view showing the whole courtyard.
page.caption: What your screenshot should show: the whole Editor, with the framed courtyard in the Game view.
page.shows: The finished screenshot opened in an image viewer. The whole Unity Editor is visible with the Courtyard scene, the Game tab selected and showing the framed courtyard, the Hierarchy listing the eight objects, and the title bar showing Courtyard. Capture on Windows or Mac, and say which.

page.text: You should now have two files on your computer: a picture of the whole Editor with the framed courtyard in the Game view, and a recording of about ten seconds in which Play is pressed and stopped. Both should open and play. If the picture shows another window, or the recording is blank or shows a different program, capture again with Unity in front.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
1. Game Bar does nothing when you press Windows and G. Fix: switch it on under **Settings** > **Gaming** as in the steps above, and click the Unity window before you press the keys. If it still will not record and you have Windows 11, use the Snipping Tool steps.

2. Game Bar says it cannot record, or the clip is black. Fix: click the Unity window first so it is active, then start again. On Windows 11 you can also use Snipping Tool instead.

3. On a Mac, you cannot find the recording. Fix: open the toolbar again with Shift, Command and 5, click **Options** and look under **Save to**.
Challenges: extend your Courtyard
These two challenges practise what you did with no steps, because building from numbers is easier once you work them out yourself. Save your scene first, and keep the Game view at 16:9 Aspect.
Challenge: close the courtyard and roof the tower

Add a Cube named Wall_Right along the right edge of the Ground, the same height and length as Wall_Left. Add a Sphere named Dome that rests exactly on top of Tower, with its lowest point touching the top of the tower. Check in your Game view that both are fully visible.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Wall_Right is a mirror of Wall_Left, so only one number changes sign. For Dome, work out how tall Tower is after scaling and where its top is. A sphere at Scale 2 is 2 units across, so its centre is one unit above its lowest point.
Optional challenge: a staircase against the back wall

Build three Cubes named Step_1, Step_2 and Step_3 on the right side of the courtyard, between Crate_A and Wall_Back. Each is 4 units wide and 2 units deep. Their tops are 1, 2 and 3 units above the ground, rising towards Wall_Back, and Step_3 touches the front face of Wall_Back. All three are centred 5 units to the right of the middle. Check that none overlaps a crate or the tower, and that all three show in your Game view.

page.title: Hint
page.text: Wall_Back is 1 unit thick and centred at Z 10, so its front face is at Z 9.5. A step 2 units deep that touches it has its centre at Z 8.5. Each next step is one step further forward, so its centre moves back by the depth. A step’s height is its Scale Y, and its centre Y is half of that.

Your Game view should still show everything. With the first challenge you should see a wall on each side and a sphere sitting on top of the tower with no gap. With the optional challenge you should see three steps rising towards the back wall on the right, clear of the crates. If a step seems to float, compare its Position Y with half its Scale Y.
Wrap-up

You can now install Unity 6.6 and Visual Studio Code, open a Universal 3D project, name the Editor’s windows and build a scene by typing Transform values. Test yourself. Install: which two things does a project need that Unity Hub holds? Windows: which window lists every object, and which shows the settings of the one you select? Build: a Cube is 1 unit tall at Scale 1; at Scale Y 3, resting on the ground, what Position Y puts it there? Next week you give these shapes components, materials and light, then roll a ball around an arena using a Rigidbody.

keyIdeas: Every GameObject is a container, and its components decide what it looks like, what is solid and how it moves. The Inspector lists them, and you can switch each one off, change it or add another.

A material is a file that says how a surface looks, and its colour is the colour box beside Base Map. A light is a component too, with a colour of its own, so what you see is the surface and the light together.

A Rigidbody hands an object to the physics engine, so gravity and collisions move it. A collider gives it a solid shape. Without a Rigidbody an object does not move, and without colliders it passes through everything.
Changes you make while Play is on are thrown away when you stop. Make your fixes while the game is stopped.

study.overview: This week you learned that a game object is a container, and that its parts decide how it looks, what is solid and how it moves. You can now open the Inspector, read the components on an object, and change them. You built the Arena from a floor and four walls, coloured it with materials and a light, and made a red-orange ball fall, roll down a ramp and bump a wall. This is the start of Orb Collector. Reread this page before next week, when you write your first script.

points.heading: Every object is a stack of components
points.explanation: A GameObject does nothing by itself. Its components do the work, and the Inspector lists them from the top. A Cube has a Transform for where it is, a Mesh Filter for its shape, a Mesh Renderer that draws it and a Box Collider that makes it solid. You can switch each one off with its checkbox, change its values, or add another with Add Component. Example: when you unticked the Mesh Renderer on Floor, the floor vanished from the Scene and Game views, but it was still there. Looks and solidity are separate jobs. When something goes wrong, select the object and read its components first.

points.heading: Materials and lights both set the colour you see
points.explanation: A material is a file that says how a surface looks. Its colour is the colour box beside Base Map, under Surface Inputs. There is no field called Albedo or Color. You made M_Floor with hexadecimal 3B4A5A and dragged it onto Floor in the Hierarchy. A light is a component with a colour of its own. On the Directional Light, set Light Appearance to Color, then use the colour box under Emission. When you typed FF8A1F, every surface turned orange. Typing FFF4E0 gave a gentle warm white. What you see is the surface and the light together, so one light can change the mood of a whole scene.

points.heading: A Rigidbody moves it, a collider makes it solid
points.explanation: A Rigidbody hands an object to the physics engine, so gravity and collisions move it. A collider gives the object a solid shape. You need both. Example: before you added a Rigidbody, the Ball hung in the air when you pressed Play. After you added one, it fell onto the Ramp and rolled to Wall_North. When you unticked the Sphere Collider, the ball still fell, but it passed through the ramp and the floor. Without a Rigidbody an object does not move. Without colliders it passes through everything. The Floor has a collider but no Rigidbody, because it should never move.

points.heading: Fix things while Play is off
points.explanation: Changes you make while Play is on are thrown away when you stop. When you changed the Ball’s Mass to 50 during Play, it read 1 again after you stopped. Use Play to watch what happens, then press Play again to stop before you fix anything. Switching one thing off at a time, such as Use Gravity or a collider, is a quick way to find which component does which job. You can use the same trick to find bugs later.

page.text: Last week you built the Courtyard from plain shapes and learned the name of every Editor window. This week those shapes start to behave. You will see that every object is a stack of components, give surfaces colour with materials, tint a light, and add a Rigidbody to a ball so that gravity and collisions move it. This is the start of Orb Collector, the first game you build. By Sunday you will have an Arena scene where a red-orange ball drops onto a ramp, rolls across a floor and bumps a wall. You will also know which component does which job.

page.text: Start the OrbCollector project

A new project keeps everything for one game in one place, and the Arena you build this week is the ground of your first game. Take a minute to see where you are heading, then watch the video on components, then make the project.

page.text: This page is written for Unity 6.6 (editor 6000.6.4f1) and the Universal 3D template. Your window title should read Unity 6.6 (6000.6.4f1), or another 6000.6 version. If your Editor is a different version, open Unity Hub, click Installs, then Install Editor and add Unity 6.6 before you go on, because menu names differ between versions. If you already made a project from another template, do not use it. Make a new one with the steps below.

page.transcript:
Welcome to the week where your shapes start to move. Last week you learned that everything in a scene is a GameObject. Here is the next idea: a GameObject by itself does almost nothing. It is an empty box with a Transform inside. Everything else it can do comes from components that you put in the box.

Take the Cube. Select it and look at the Inspector. Transform says where it is. Mesh Filter holds its shape. Mesh Renderer draws that shape on screen. Box Collider is the solid shape that other objects bump into. Four components, four jobs. If you switch off the Mesh Renderer, the cube disappears from view, but the Box Collider is still there. You cannot see it, but it is still solid. Looking like something and being solid are separate jobs.

Next, materials. A material is a file in your Project window that says how a surface looks. Its colour is the colour box beside Base Map. You make one material, such as a floor material, and drop it on any object. Change the colour once and every object that uses it changes. Lights are components too. A Directional Light has its own colour. What you see on screen is the surface colour and the light colour together.

Now physics. Add a Rigidbody component to an object and you hand it to Unity’s physics engine. Gravity pulls it down, speeding it up by about 9.8 metres per second, every second. When it meets something solid it stops, bounces or rolls. But the engine can only do that if both things have colliders. The Rigidbody says, move me. The collider says, here is my shape. You need both.

One surprise. A heavy ball and a light ball fall at the same speed, because gravity pulls harder on heavy things but they are harder to move too. You will test that yourself.

One warning. When you press Play, anything you change in the Inspector is thrown away when you press Play again to stop. Fix things while the game is stopped.

Now build the Arena.

page.text: Build the arena and read its components
You will place a floor and four walls by exact numbers, then look inside them. Reading an object’s components is how you find out what it can do, and how you will fix almost every problem this term.

The numbers come from the same arithmetic as last week. A Cube is 1 unit tall at Scale 1, and Position is its centre. The Floor has Scale Y of 1, so its centre sits at Y of −0.5 and its top face is at Y of 0. The walls are 2 units tall, so their centre is at Y of 1 and they stand on the floor. Wall_North and Wall_South are 22 long, so they cover the corners that Wall_East and Wall_West leave open.

items.text: Choose **GameObject > 3D Object > Cube**.
Type Floor and press Enter.
In the **Inspector**, in the **Transform** section, set **Position** to 0, −0.5, 0. A new object appears wherever the Scene view is looking, so always type all three numbers.

shot.alt: Floor Transform: Position 0, -0.5, 0; Rotation 0, 0, 0; Scale 20, 1, 20.
shot.shows: The Inspector for Floor, Transform section only, with Position 0, -0.5, 0 and Scale 20, 1, 20 visible. Outline the Position and Scale rows.

items.text: Set **Scale** to 20, 1, 20. Leave **Rotation** at 0, 0, 0.
Choose **GameObject > 3D Object > Cube**, type Wall_North and press Enter.
Set **Position** to 0, 1, 10.5 and **Scale** to 22, 2, 1.
Choose **GameObject > 3D Object > Cube**, type Wall_South and press Enter.
Set **Position** to 0, 1, −10.5 and **Scale** to 22, 2, 1.
Choose **GameObject > 3D Object > Cube**, type Wall_East and press Enter.
Set **Position** to 10.5, 1, 0 and **Scale** to 1, 2, 20.
Choose **GameObject > 3D Object > Cube**, type Wall_West and press Enter.
Set **Position** to −10.5, 1, 0 and **Scale** to 1, 2, 20.
In the **Hierarchy** window, click **Main Camera**.
In the **Inspector**, set **Position** to 0, 16, −16 and **Rotation** to 45, 0, 0.
Click the **Game** tab and check that the shape dropdown at its top left reads **16:9 Aspect**.
Choose **File > Save**.

shot.alt: Game view of a grey-white floor ringed by four walls, with the Hierarchy listing Floor, Wall_North, Wall_South, Wall_East and Wall_West.
shot.shows: The Game view at 16:9 Aspect showing the whole arena from above and in front, all objects the default grey-white. Hierarchy visible at left with Floor and the four walls listed.

page.title: Shortcut
page.text: To save time, click Wall_North and choose Edit > Duplicate (Ctrl+D on Windows, Command+D on a Mac), then rename the copy and change its numbers. A duplicate keeps every component of the original.
Now look inside. Everything you just made is a stack of components, and the Inspector lists them from the top.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy** window, click **Floor**.

In the **Inspector**, find the components in order: **Transform**, **Mesh Filter**, **Mesh Renderer** and **Box Collider**. At the bottom is the material, **Lit (Material)**, greyed out because the default material cannot be edited.

shot.alt: Inspector for Floor listing Transform, Mesh Filter, Mesh Renderer and Box Collider, with Lit (Material) greyed out below and the Add Component button at the bottom.
shot.shows: The Inspector for Floor with all four component headings visible, Mesh Renderer and Box Collider included. Outline the checkbox beside Mesh Renderer.

items.text: Untick the checkbox at the left of the **Mesh Renderer** heading. The floor vanishes from the Scene view and the Game view.
Tick the checkbox again. The floor comes back.
Click the **Add Component** button, type Rigidbody, and press **Escape** to close the box without adding anything. Floor stays as it is.

page.title: Why this matters
page.text: The Mesh Filter holds the shape, the Mesh Renderer draws it, and the Box Collider is the solid shape that physics uses. You switched off the drawing and nothing else changed, so appearance and solidity are separate jobs. A Floor does not need a Rigidbody, because it should never move.

The Game view shows the whole floor and all four walls, still in plain grey-white, from above and in front. Floor is switched on again: its Mesh Renderer box is ticked. It went wrong if part of the arena is cut off (check the camera Position and Rotation), if a wall floats or sinks into the floor (check its Position Y is 1) or if the floor is missing (tick the Mesh Renderer).

page.alt: The grey-white arena fully in view with Floor selected, showing Transform, Mesh Filter, Mesh Renderer and Box Collider in the Inspector.
page.shows: The Game view at 16:9 Aspect with the finished grey arena, and the Inspector open beside it on Floor with its four components visible.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
A wall is in the wrong place: you probably typed only one Position number. Type X, Y and Z every time, because a new object does not start at 0, 0, 0.

There is a gap at a corner: Wall_North and Wall_South need Scale X of 22, not 20.

The Game view looks different from this page: check the aspect dropdown reads 16:9 Aspect and the camera numbers match.
Colour the arena with materials
Plain grey makes every surface look the same, and the default material cannot be edited. A material of your own lets you choose a colour, and one material can be shared by many objects.

A new material uses the shader Universal Render Pipeline/Lit. A shader is the small program that decides how light falls on a surface. In this shader the colour of a material is the colour box beside **Base Map**. There is no field called Albedo or Color. You will make four materials with these colours:

items: M_Floor, hexadecimal 3B4A5A (a dark slate)
M_Wall, hexadecimal 9AA5B1 (a light grey-blue)
M_Ramp, hexadecimal F2B134 (a warm yellow)
M_Ball, hexadecimal E8503A (a bright red-orange)

items.text: In the **Project** window, click the **Assets** folder.
Choose **Assets > Create > Folder**, type Materials and press Enter.
Double-click the **Materials** folder to open it.
Choose **Assets > Create > Material**, type M_Floor and press Enter.
With M_Floor selected, in the **Inspector** find **Surface Inputs** and click the colour box beside **Base Map**.

shot.alt: Surface Inputs section of M_Floor: Base Map with a colour box beside it, then Metallic Map, Smoothness 0.5, Normal Map.
shot.shows: The Inspector for M_Floor with Surface Inputs open. Outline the colour box beside Base Map.

items.text: In the window titled **Color**, click the **Hexadecimal** box, type 3B4A5A and press Enter. Close the window.

shot.shows: The Color window opened from the Base Map box, with the mode showing RGB 0-255 and the Hexadecimal box containing 3B4A5A. Outline the Hexadecimal box.

items.text: Make three more materials the same way: M_Wall with 9AA5B1, M_Ramp with F2B134 and M_Ball with E8503A. Each time choose **Assets > Create > Material** first.
Select M_Ball and drag the **Smoothness** slider to 0.8 so it looks shiny.
Drag M_Floor from the **Project** window onto **Floor** in the **Hierarchy**.
Drag M_Wall from the **Project** window onto **Wall_North** in the **Hierarchy**, then onto **Wall_South**, **Wall_East** and **Wall_West** in turn.

Click Floor: the material at the bottom of its Inspector now reads M_Floor and is no longer greyed out. page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
The colour did not change: you clicked a different box. Use the colour box beside Base Map, under Surface Inputs.

The Color window has no Hexadecimal box: make the window taller, or check the mode dropdown reads RGB 0-255.

Only one wall changed colour: drag the material onto each wall in turn, or select all four walls in the Hierarchy with Ctrl (Windows) or Command (Mac) held and drag once.
Light the arena
A light is a component too, and it has a colour of its own. What you see is the surface colour and the light colour together, so you will tint the light and watch every surface change.

items.text: In the **Hierarchy** window, click **Directional Light**.
In the **Inspector**, find the **Light** component. It has four sections that open with a triangle: **General**, **Emission**, **Rendering** and **Shadows**.
Click the triangle beside **Emission** to open it.
Find **Light Appearance**, which reads **Filter and Temperature**. Open its dropdown and choose **Color**.

shot.alt: Emission section of the Directional Light: Light Appearance set to Color, a colour box, and Intensity 2.
shot.shows: The Inspector for Directional Light with the Emission section open. Outline the Light Appearance dropdown showing Color and the colour box.

items.text: Click the colour box that now shows in the **Emission** section.
In the window titled **Color**, click the **Hexadecimal** box, type FF8A1F and press Enter. Look at the Game view: every surface turns orange.

shot.alt: Arena tinted orange by the Directional Light set to FF8A1F, with the Color window open.
shot.shows: The Game view beside the Color window at the moment the light is FF8A1F, so the orange tint on the floor and walls is visible.

items.text: Click the colour box again, type FFF4E0 in the **Hexadecimal** box and press Enter. The light is now a gentle warm white.
Check that **Intensity** reads 2 and leave it there.
Choose **File > Save**.

page.title: Why the orange test
page.text: You changed one number on one light and every material looked different. Light colour multiplies surface colour, so a slate floor under an orange light is a warm dark colour. That is why games change the mood of a whole scene by changing the lights alone.

The floor and walls look like their material colours with a slight warm cast, and the walls cast shadows across the floor. The Light Appearance reads Color and Intensity reads 2. It went wrong if the arena is still orange (repeat the colour step with FFF4E0) or if no colour box shows (Light Appearance is still Filter and Temperature).

page.alt: The lit arena in the Game view; the Directional Light shows Light Appearance Color and Intensity 2.
page.shows: The Game view at 16:9 Aspect with the lit arena, and the Inspector beside it on Directional Light with Emission open.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
You cannot find the colour box: open the Emission section with its triangle, then set Light Appearance to Color.

Nothing changed in the Game view: check you selected Directional Light, not Main Camera.

The scene is far too dark or too bright: set Intensity back to 2.
Make the ball and the ramp, and add a Rigidbody
A Rigidbody is the component that lets physics move an object. You will first see a ball that does nothing, then add the Rigidbody and watch gravity and the ramp do the work.

The ramp is a Cube tilted 20 degrees. A positive Rotation X tips its far end, the +Z end, downward, so a ball landing on it rolls towards Wall_North. The Ramp is 10 long and 0.4 thick, centred at Y of 2, so its low end sits just above the floor and its high end is near 4. The ball starts at Y of 6, a little above the high part, so it falls onto the ramp.

items.text: Choose **GameObject > 3D Object > Cube** and type Ramp.
Set **Position** to 0, 2, −4, **Rotation** to 20, 0, 0 and **Scale** to 6, 0.4, 10.
Drag M_Ramp from the **Materials** folder onto **Ramp** in the **Hierarchy**.
Choose **GameObject > 3D Object > Sphere** and type Ball.

shot.alt: Yellow Ramp tilted down towards the far wall with the red-orange Ball above it; Hierarchy lists Ramp and Ball.
shot.shows: The Scene view with Ramp and Ball placed above it, the Ramp tilted, and the Hierarchy listing Ramp and Ball. Outline the Ball above the high part of the Ramp.

items.text: Set **Position** to 0, 6, −7 and leave **Scale** at 1, 1, 1.
Drag M_Ball from the **Materials** folder onto **Ball** in the **Hierarchy**.
With **Ball** selected, look at the **Inspector**: it has **Transform**, **Mesh Filter**, **Mesh Renderer** and **Sphere Collider**, but no Rigidbody.
Click the **Play** button at the top centre of the Editor. The ball hangs in the air and nothing moves. Click **Play** again to stop.
Click **Add Component**, type Rigidbody and choose **Rigidbody** from the list, not Rigidbody 2D.

shot.alt: Ball Inspector: Sphere Collider, then Rigidbody with Mass 1, Linear Damping 0, Angular Damping 0.05, Use Gravity ticked.
shot.shows: The Inspector for Ball after Add Component, with the Rigidbody section open and Sphere Collider above it. Outline the Rigidbody heading, Mass and Use Gravity.

items.text: Look at the new **Rigidbody** section: **Mass** 1, **Linear Damping** 0, **Angular Damping** 0.05 and **Use Gravity** ticked.
Click **Play**. The ball falls onto the ramp, rolls down, crosses the floor and stops at Wall_North. Click **Play** again to stop.
Choose **File > Save**.

page.alt: First the ball stays still in the air. After a Rigidbody is added, it falls onto the ramp, rolls down, crosses the floor and stops at the far wall.
page.shows: The Game view and the top of the Editor so the Play button is visible. First press Play with no Rigidbody on Ball and let it hang for three seconds, stop, add the Rigidbody, then press Play again and let the ball roll to the far wall.

page.title: The Rigidbody fields
page.text: Mass is how heavy the ball is to the physics engine. Use Gravity pulls the ball down. Linear Damping is a brake on moving; at 0 there is none. There are no fields called Drag or Angular Drag in this version.

Before you added the Rigidbody, the ball stayed where it was. After you added it, the ball fell onto the ramp, rolled down it, crossed the floor and came to rest against Wall_North. It went wrong if the ball falls through the ramp (the Sphere Collider is switched off), if it never moves (the Rigidbody is missing, or you added Rigidbody 2D) or if it rolls off to the side (check the Ramp Rotation is 20, 0, 0).

page.alt: The red-orange Ball rolling down the yellow Ramp in the lit Arena during Play.
page.shows: The Game view during Play with the ball halfway down the ramp, and the Hierarchy visible with Ramp and Ball.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
The ball never moves when you press Play: it has no Rigidbody. Add Component, type Rigidbody and pick Rigidbody, not Rigidbody 2D.

The ball falls through the ramp or floor: its Sphere Collider is unticked, or the Ramp’s Box Collider is unticked. Tick them.

The ball misses the ramp: check the Ball Position is 0, 6, −7 and the Ramp Position is 0, 2, −4.
Test what a Rigidbody and a collider each do
You now have a working scene, so you will break it on purpose. Switching one thing off at a time is the fastest way to learn which component does which job, and the same trick finds bugs later.

items.text: Make sure Play is off. Click **Ball** in the **Hierarchy**.
In the **Rigidbody** section, untick **Use Gravity**. Click **Play**. The ball hangs in the air. Click **Play** to stop, then tick **Use Gravity** again.

Untick the checkbox at the left of the **Sphere Collider** heading. Click **Play**. The ball falls straight through the ramp and the floor and keeps going. Click **Play** to stop, then tick the box again.

shot.alt: Ball Inspector with the Sphere Collider heading unticked and the Rigidbody section below it.
shot.shows: The Inspector for Ball with the Sphere Collider checkbox unticked and the Rigidbody section below it. Outline the Sphere Collider checkbox.

items.text: Click **Ball**, choose **Edit > Duplicate**, and type Ball_Heavy as its name.
Set the **Position** of Ball_Heavy to 2, 6, −7 and its **Mass** to 10.
Click **Ball** and set its **Position** to −2, 6, −7.
Click **Play** and watch both balls. They land and roll together, side by side. Click **Play** to stop.

shot.alt: Two balls, Ball and Ball_Heavy, rolling down the ramp side by side at the same height.
shot.shows: The Game view during Play with Ball and Ball_Heavy side by side on the ramp at the same height. Outline both balls.

items.text: Click **Play** again. While it runs, click **Ball** and change **Mass** to 50.
Click **Play** to stop, then click **Ball**. **Mass** reads 1 again, because changes made during Play are thrown away.
Click **Ball_Heavy** and choose **Edit > Delete**.
Click **Ball** and set its **Position** back to 0, 6, −7.
Choose **File > Save**.

page.title: What you learned
page.text: Without gravity the Rigidbody has no reason to move. Without the collider, the Rigidbody still falls, but nothing is solid enough to stop it. A heavier ball keeps up with a light one because gravity pulls harder on it and it is harder to move by the same amount.

The Hierarchy lists Floor, four walls, Ramp, Ball and the camera and light, but no Ball_Heavy. Ball has Mass 1, Use Gravity ticked and Sphere Collider ticked, at Position 0, 6, −7. Pressing Play shows the ball roll down the ramp again. It went wrong if the ball falls through things (a collider is still unticked) or if Mass is not 1.

page.alt: Ball Inspector: Sphere Collider on, Rigidbody Mass 1, Use Gravity ticked; Hierarchy has no Ball_Heavy.
page.shows: The Inspector for Ball showing Sphere Collider ticked and Rigidbody with Mass 1 and Use Gravity ticked, with the Hierarchy at left.

page.title: Stuck?
page.text:
Mass is not 1 after Play: a change made during Play should reset when you stop. With Play off, select Ball rather than Ball_Heavy and set Mass to 1.

The balls do not land together: check both Positions have Y of 6 and Z of −7.

page.shows: The OrbCollector project as it should stand after this part: the Arena scene with Floor, four walls, Ramp and Ball, the materials M_Floor, M_Wall, M_Ramp and M_Ball, a warm white Directional Light, and a Rigidbody on Ball. Use it to compare, or to carry on if something went wrong.

page.text: Challenges
These two challenges have no steps, because working things out yourself is how the components stick. Save the Arena first. Keep Play off while you change things.

Challenge: a bouncy ball. Add a second sphere named Ball_Bouncy at Position 6, 6, 4, with the M_Ball material and a Rigidbody. Make it bounce, so that when you press Play it falls onto the floor and bounces at least three times, each bounce lower than the last, before settling. The ramp does not reach that spot, so only the floor is in its way.

page.title: Hint
page.text: A bounce comes from a physics material on the ball’s collider. Make one with Assets > Create > Physics Material, name it PM_Bouncy, and raise its Bounciness to 0.8. Drag it onto the Material box of the Sphere Collider, which reads None (Physics Material). If the bounces are weak, the floor has no material so the bounce is averaged: set Bounce Combine on PM_Bouncy to Maximum.

Optional challenge: a lamp in the arena. Turn the arena into a dim room with one lamp. Lower the Directional Light Intensity to 0.4. Add a Point Light named Lamp (GameObject > Light > Point Light) at Position 0, 4, 3 with a warm yellow colour. The floor and the ramp’s low end should glow near the lamp and the corners of the arena should look darker. Press Play and check the ball still rolls the same way.

page.title: Hint
page.text: A Point Light shines in all directions from one spot, and its Light component has the same Emission section as the Directional Light, with a Light Appearance setting for its colour. Look through the Light component for a Range value and raise it until the glow reaches the walls.

Your Ball_Bouncy bounces several times, each lower than the last. If you tried the optional challenge, your Lamp makes a bright patch near the middle of the floor while the far corners stay dark. The main Ball still rolls down the ramp. It went wrong if Ball_Bouncy does not bounce (the physics material is not on its Sphere Collider) or if nothing glows (Lamp Intensity is too low or Range too small).

page.alt: Ball_Bouncy mid-bounce in a dimmed Arena with a warm patch of light on the floor.
page.shows: The Game view during Play with Ball_Bouncy mid-bounce above the floor and the Lamp glow visible on the floor, and the Inspector showing the Sphere Collider Material box with PM_Bouncy.

page.text: Wrap-up

You can now add, switch off and read components in the Inspector, make a material and set its colour and a light’s colour, and make a ball fall and roll with a Rigidbody and colliders. Test yourself. Components: which two components give a Cube its looks and its solidity? Colour: which box sets a material’s colour, and what changes if you recolour the light? Physics: what happens to a Rigidbody ball with no collider, and what happens to a change you make during Play? Next time you write your first script, with variables, Start and Update, to spin an object, and you learn to read an error in the Console.

t_0cb83ea709b9.prompt: A Cube has Scale Y set to 4. What Position Y places it on a flat ground at Y = 0, with its bottom resting on the ground?

f_b2f946aa0fb7.question: Unity Hub says there is no license, or a project refuses to open. What do I do?
f_b2f946aa0fb7.answer: The license is probably missing or tied to a different Unity ID. First, in Unity Hub click the gear at the top right, choose Licenses, and look for a Unity Personal license. Second, if the list is empty, click Add license, choose the free Unity Personal option and follow the prompts. Third, check that you are signed in with the same Unity ID you used before. Fourth, open the project again from Projects. If it still will not open, ask in the course Q&A forum and say which step you reached.

f_6f4964bdb59f.question: The download or install stops moving, or the Installs list shows it as failed. What do I do?
f_6f4964bdb59f.answer: Large downloads fail when the connection drops or the disk is nearly full. First, check that your internet is working and that you have about 20 GB of free disk space. Second, in Installs, use the retry option on the entry, or click Install Editor again and choose the same version. The install resumes where it stopped. Third, if 6.6 is not listed, use the download archive link on that screen, find 6000.6.4 and click its install button. Fourth, if your computer belongs to a school or employer and blocks the install, ask its IT help desk to install Unity Hub and Unity 6.6. If none of this works, ask in the course Q&A forum.

f_7d967ab62f1d.question: The Editor looks frozen after I click Create project, or my title bar shows another version. What do I do?
f_7d967ab62f1d.answer: If the Editor looks frozen, the first open compiles and imports files and can take five minutes or more. Wait until the progress bar at the bottom of the window is gone. If the title bar does not read like SampleScene - Courtyard - Windows, Mac, Linux - Unity 6.6 (6000.6.4f1), you made the project with the wrong version or template. First, close the Editor. Second, in Unity Hub click New project and check that the Editor version at the top reads 6000.6.4f1 or another 6000.6 version. Third, open the dropdown beside the search box, choose Core and click Universal 3D. Fourth, create the project again as a local project. If creating keeps failing, download the starter project from this page. Ask in the course Q&A forum if that fails too.

f_383feedef9f8.question: My Courtyard looks wrong: an object floats, sinks or lies flat, or the Game view is cropped or cut off. What do I do?
f_383feedef9f8.answer: The cause is almost always one number in the Transform or the camera. First, click the object in the Hierarchy and compare its Position, Rotation and Scale with the list on this page. A new object appears where the Scene view is looking, so every value must be typed. Second, check that Position Y is half the object’s height after scaling. Third, if you cannot see an object in the Scene view, click it in the Hierarchy, move the pointer over the Scene view and press F. Fourth, if the Game view is cut off, click the Game tab and choose 16:9 Aspect. Then select Main Camera and check that Position is 0, 16, -16, Rotation is 45, 0, 0 and Field of View is 60. If it still does not match, open the finished project from this page and compare. Ask in the course Q&A forum and attach a screenshot.

f_78d767e76c96.question: I cannot find Universal 3D in Unity Hub. What do I do?
f_78d767e76c96.answer: You see only the Learning templates. 1. In Unity Hub, click Projects, then New project. 2. Open the dropdown beside the search box. 3. Choose Core. 4. Click Universal 3D. Also check that the Editor version at the top reads 6000.6.4f1, or another 6000.6 version. If it does not, click Installs, then Install Editor, and add Unity 6.6. If the fix does not work, ask in the course Q&A forum.

f_27f5744c8bd3.question: The ball just hangs in the air when I press Play, or it falls straight through the ramp. Why?
f_27f5744c8bd3.answer: If the ball never moves, it has no Rigidbody. 1. Stop Play. 2. Click Ball in the Hierarchy. 3. Click Add Component, type Rigidbody and choose Rigidbody, not Rigidbody 2D. 4. Check that Use Gravity is ticked. If the ball falls through the ramp or floor, a collider is switched off. 1. Stop Play. 2. Tick the checkbox beside Sphere Collider on Ball. 3. Tick the checkbox beside Box Collider on Ramp and Floor. If the ball misses the ramp, check that Ball is at Position 0, 6, −7 and Ramp is at 0, 2, −4. If it still behaves wrongly, ask in the course Q&A forum.

f_8988c99fca08.question: I changed a value while the game was running, and it went back when I stopped. What happened?
f_8988c99fca08.answer: Changes made during Play are thrown away when you stop. This is how Unity works, so nothing is broken. 1. Click Play again to stop the game. The Play button is no longer lit. 2. Select the object in the Hierarchy. 3. Type the value again in the Inspector. 4. Choose File > Save. Make every fix while Play is off. If a value will not stay, ask in the course Q&A forum.

f_4c1722fdb1ad.question: My material colour will not change, or the walls are still grey. How do I fix it?
f_4c1722fdb1ad.answer: If the colour will not change, you probably clicked a different box. 1. Select the material in the Project window. 2. In the Inspector, find Surface Inputs. 3. Click the colour box beside Base Map. 4. In the Color window, click the Hexadecimal box, type the code and press Enter. If the Hexadecimal box is missing, make the window taller and check that the mode dropdown reads RGB 0-255. If an object is still grey, the drag missed it. Drag the material from the Project window onto the object’s name in the Hierarchy, once for each wall. If the colour still will not change, ask in the course Q&A forum.

# Instructor's version notes: Unity 6.6 (editor 6000.6.4), checked in the editor

Use these names exactly. They are what students see on screen.

## Unity Hub
- Sidebar: Projects, Templates, Installs. Settings is the gear at the top right; licenses are under Settings > Licenses > Add license.
- Projects > New project. The screen opens on the "Learning" templates. Open the dropdown beside the search box and choose "Core" to see Universal 2D, Universal 3D, High Definition 3D and others. The Editor version is chosen at the top of this screen.
- With a template selected, the panel on the right shows: Unity organization, Project name, Location, Use AI Assistant, Use Unity CLI, Source control provider, and the Create project button.
- The Project name box is also a dropdown: "Create new project" (connected to Unity Cloud, the default) or "Create new local project". Students choose "Create new local project", then type the name.
- Clicking Location opens a folder picker with a "Select folder" button.

## A new Universal 3D project
- The window title reads: SampleScene - <project name> - Windows, Mac, Linux - Unity 6.6 (6000.6.4f1).
- Hierarchy: SampleScene with Main Camera, Directional Light and Global Volume.
- Project window, Assets folder: InputSystem_Actions, Readme, Scenes, Settings, TutorialInfo. The scene file is Assets/Scenes/SampleScene.
- On first open the Inspector shows a "URP Empty Template" readme with a "Remove Readme Assets" button.
- Windows in the Default layout: Hierarchy (left), Scene and Game tabs (centre), Inspector (right), Project and Console tabs (bottom). Reset with Window > Layouts > Default.

## Menus (top menu bar)
- File: New Scene, Open Scene, Save, Save As..., Build Profiles, Build And Run. There is no "Build Settings" item: the build window is File > Build Profiles.
- Edit: Undo, Redo, Duplicate, Rename, Delete, Play Mode, Project Settings... On a Mac, preferences are Unity > Settings...; on Windows, Edit > Preferences...
- GameObject: Create Empty, Create Empty Child, 2D Object, 3D Object, Visual Effects, Light, Audio, UI Toolkit, UI (Canvas), Camera.
- GameObject > 3D Object: Cube, Sphere, Capsule, Cylinder, Plane, Quad, Text - TextMeshPro.
- GameObject > UI (Canvas): Image, Text - TextMeshPro, Panel, Button - TextMeshPro, Toggle, Slider, Canvas, Event System. The menu is named "UI (Canvas)", not "UI".
- GameObject > Visual Effects: Particle System, Trail, Line. GameObject > Audio: Audio Source. GameObject > Light: Directional Light, Point Light, Spot Light.
- Assets > Create: Folder, Material, MonoBehaviour Script, Scene, Scripting, Physics Material, Input Actions, Animation, 2D, TextMeshPro. A new script is Assets > Create > MonoBehaviour Script (also under Scripting > MonoBehaviour Script). A scene is Assets > Create > Scene > Scene; a prefab is made by dragging an object from the Hierarchy into the Project window.
- Assets > Create > Animation: Animator Controller, Animation Clip. Window > Animation: Animation, Animator.
- Component > Physics: Rigidbody, Box Collider, Sphere Collider, Capsule Collider, Mesh Collider. Component > Physics 2D: Rigidbody 2D, Box Collider 2D, Circle Collider 2D, Capsule Collider 2D, Composite Collider 2D.
- Window: Layouts, General (Scene, Game, Inspector, Hierarchy, Project, Console), Animation, Audio, Package Management (Package Manager), Rendering, TextMeshPro.

## Code (C#), compiled in this version
- Input: new projects use the Input System package only. `Input.GetAxis`, `Input.GetKey` and the rest of the old Input class compile but throw InvalidOperationException when the game runs. Read keys with `Keyboard.current.aKey.isPressed`, `Keyboard.current.spaceKey.wasPressedThisFrame` (with `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;`), or use the project's own actions: `InputSystem.actions.FindAction("Move")` then `ReadValue<Vector2>()`. The template's InputSystem_Actions asset has a Player map with Move, Look, Attack, Interact, Crouch, Jump, Previous, Next, Sprint.
- Rigidbody: `rb.linearVelocity` and `rb.linearDamping`. `rb.velocity` is marked obsolete.
- Finding objects: `FindAnyObjectByType<T>()`. `FindFirstObjectByType<T>()` and `FindObjectOfType<T>()` are both marked obsolete in 6000.6 and give a yellow warning.
- Text: `using TMPro;` and `TMP_Text`. Scenes: `using UnityEngine.SceneManagement;` and `SceneManager.LoadScene(...)`.
- `AddForce`, `ForceMode.Impulse`, `OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)`, `CompareTag`, `Destroy`, `Instantiate`, `Time.deltaTime`, `[SerializeField]` are unchanged.

## The Inspector, as it reads in this version
- A new object made from the GameObject menu appears where the Scene view is looking, not at the origin: its Position is some uneven number. Students type 0, 0, 0 into Position (or use the three-dot menu on Transform > Reset) before the page gives positions.
- After creating an object or asset its name is in edit mode: type the name and press Enter.
- Every object: name box, Static, Tag, Layer; then Transform with Position, Rotation, Scale (X, Y, Z each).
- A primitive (Cube, Sphere...) has: Transform, a Mesh Filter, Mesh Renderer (Materials, Lighting, Probes, Additional Settings), and its collider (Box Collider, Sphere Collider...). At the bottom is the material, "Lit (Material)", greyed out because the default material cannot be edited, and the Add Component button.
- Sphere Collider: Edit Collider, Is Trigger, Provides Contacts, Material (shows "None (Physics Material)"), Center, Radius, Layer Overrides.
- Add Component opens a small search box: type the name and press Enter. Typing "Rigidbody" lists Rigidbody and Rigidbody 2D.
- Rigidbody: Mass (1), Linear Damping (0), Angular Damping (0.05), Automatic Center Of Mass, Automatic Tensor, Use Gravity (ticked), Is Kinematic, Interpolate (None), Collision Detection (Discrete), Constraints (Freeze Position X Y Z, Freeze Rotation X Y Z), Layer Overrides. There are no fields named "Drag" or "Angular Drag".
- A new material (Assets > Create > Material) uses the shader Universal Render Pipeline/Lit. Its Inspector has Surface Options (Workflow Mode, Surface Type, Render Face, Alpha Clipping, Receive Shadows), Surface Inputs (Base Map with a colour box beside it, Metallic Map with a slider, Smoothness with a slider at 0.5, Normal Map, Height Map, Occlusion Map, Emission, Tiling, Offset), Detail Inputs and Advanced Options. The colour of a material is the colour box beside Base Map; there is no field called "Albedo" or "Color".
- Clicking a colour box opens a window titled "Color": a colour wheel, a mode dropdown showing "RGB 0-255", sliders R, G, B, A, a box labelled "Hexadecimal", and "Defaults" swatches. The box is "Hexadecimal", not "Hex Color".
- A material is put on an object by dragging it from the Project window onto the object in the Scene view or the Hierarchy.
- Directional Light: Transform (Position 0, 3, 0; Rotation 50, -30, 0), then Light with four sections that open with a triangle: General (Type: Directional, Mode: Realtime), Emission, Rendering, Shadows. Under Emission: Light Appearance (set to "Filter and Temperature"), Filter (a colour box), Temperature (a slider, 5000 Kelvin), Intensity (2), Indirect Multiplier, Cookie. To give the light a plain colour, set Light Appearance to "Color". There is also a component named Universal Additional Light Data.
- The Scene view has a column of tools at its top left (View, Move, Rotate, Scale, Rect, Transform; keys Q, W, E, R, T, Y) and the scene gizmo at its top right with "Persp" under it. Play, Pause and Step are at the top centre of the Editor.
- If a script uses an older API, Unity may show a "Script Updating Consent" dialog offering to update the files: students following the page's code should not see it.
